question.question: An adult at high refeeding risk has severely low phosphate before enteral feeding is started. Which plan best follows the 2020 ASPEN consensus?
choices: Correct the severe deficiency and delay starting or increasing calories until corrected
Start the full energy target while waiting for the next scheduled phosphate result
Advance to full energy as long as baseline potassium is normal
Ignore the phosphate result because the calories will enter through the gut
question.rationale: Severely low phosphate, potassium, or magnesium calls for delaying calorie initiation or increases until corrected under the 2020 ASPEN consensus. Enteral calories can trigger refeeding physiology, and a normal potassium result does not resolve a severe phosphate deficit. Use cautious advancement and close monitoring rather than starting at the full target.

choicesReviewed.review: Severely low phosphate is explicit: delay calorie initiation/increase until corrected.

choicesReviewed.text: Ignore the phosphate result because the calories will enter through the gut
choicesReviewed.review: Enteral calories can trigger refeeding; route does not exclude the risk.

question.question: A critically ill adult receiving gastric enteral nutrition has no contraindication to head elevation. Which positioning measure belongs in the aspiration-prevention bundle?
choices: Elevate the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees when clinically feasible
Keep the patient supine because the feeding tube tip was confirmed in the stomach
Omit head elevation because endotracheal intubation prevents all aspiration
Replace positioning and sedation review with routine residual checks alone
question.rationale: The 2016 SCCM/ASPEN adult ICU guidance recommends head elevation of 30 to 45 degrees for intubated patients receiving enteral nutrition. Proper tube position, sedation review, and assessment of aspiration risk remain necessary. Intubation does not prevent small-volume aspiration, and residual checks do not replace the bundle.

question.question: An adult ICU patient is stable without vasopressors and has a gastric residual of 350 mL without vomiting, pain, distention, or other intolerance signs. Under the 2016 SCCM/ASPEN guidance, how should this value be used?
choices: Avoid an automatic feeding hold while reassessing tolerance and aspiration precautions
Automatically hold feeding until the residual is zero despite the absence of other findings
Use the value below 500 mL as proof that aspiration precautions are unnecessary
Apply the same 500 mL rule to neonatal feeding without assessing the population
question.rationale: The 2016 adult ICU guideline advises against automatically holding feeding for residuals below 500 mL without other intolerance signs. Values from 200 to 500 mL still raise concern and warrant measures to reduce aspiration risk. This is a population-specific recommendation, not proof of normal tolerance or a neonatal threshold; vasopressor guidance may use a different approach.

question.question: During the first two days of enteral feeding in a malnourished adult, phosphate, potassium, and magnesium fall substantially from baseline. Which interpretation best fits this pattern?
choices: Treat it as a refeeding warning and promptly evaluate the electrolyte changes and energy exposure
Exclude refeeding because the baseline serum electrolytes were normal
Exclude refeeding because nutrition was delivered enterally rather than intravenously
Correct phosphate alone and disregard the concurrent potassium and magnesium changes
question.rationale: Refeeding can cause substantial decreases in phosphate, potassium, and magnesium after calories are reintroduced. Normal initial serum concentrations do not exclude total-body depletion, and enteral nutrition is a possible trigger. Assess all three electrolytes, the clinical condition, other causes, and energy delivery rather than dismissing the pattern or addressing phosphate alone.

choicesReviewed.text: Treat it as a refeeding warning and promptly evaluate the electrolyte changes and energy exposure
choicesReviewed.review: Temporal three-electrolyte fall is a warning requiring evaluation of all electrolytes, clinical state, energy and other causes.

choicesReviewed.text: Exclude refeeding because the baseline serum electrolytes were normal
choicesReviewed.review: Normal baseline serum values do not exclude total-body depletion.

choicesReviewed.text: Exclude refeeding because nutrition was delivered enterally rather than intravenously
choicesReviewed.review: Enteral feeding is a possible refeeding exposure.

choicesReviewed.text: Correct phosphate alone and disregard the concurrent potassium and magnesium changes
choicesReviewed.review: Concurrent potassium/magnesium falls must not be disregarded.

question.question: An adult with a newly used jejunostomy develops cramping and diarrhea during four rapid 400 mL boluses. Placement has been confirmed, and the nutrition team is reviewing delivery tolerance. What is the best next action?
choices: Reassess the regimen and use controlled pump delivery with an individualized rate and schedule
Repeat the same rapid boluses without reviewing the rate or symptoms
Use gastric bolus tolerance as proof that this jejunal regimen must be tolerated
Commit to continuous feeding 24 hours daily indefinitely without reassessment
question.rationale: The 2017 ASPEN safe-practice guidance recommends matching the schedule to patient condition, tolerance, goals, and tube destination. Jejunal feeding may be better tolerated as periodic continuous feeding; this symptomatic new regimen warrants controlled delivery and reassessment. The case does not establish a universal lifelong schedule or a rule prohibiting every adult jejunal bolus.

question.question: Within 48 hours of restarting enteral feeding in a malnourished adult, phosphate falls rapidly from 3.0 to 1.2 mg/dL and is difficult to correct. What is the best next action?
choices: Urgently assess and treat the electrolyte abnormality and reduce calorie delivery while evaluating refeeding and other causes
Continue the same calorie delivery because the initial phosphate was normal
Increase calorie delivery to correct the low phosphate without electrolyte treatment
Exclude refeeding because the calories were delivered through a feeding tube
question.rationale: A precipitous phosphate decline after calorie reintroduction is a major refeeding warning, even with a normal baseline level. The 2020 ASPEN consensus recommends reducing calorie or dextrose delivery when electrolytes fall precipitously or are difficult to correct, together with prompt treatment and monitoring. Severe or life-threatening abnormalities may require stopping nutrition temporarily under clinical judgment; the laboratory value does not by itself exclude other causes.

choicesReviewed.text: Urgently assess and treat the electrolyte abnormality and reduce calorie delivery while evaluating refeeding and other causes
choicesReviewed.review: Rapid hard-to-correct fall after restarting calories warrants urgent treatment/assessment and energy reduction.

choicesReviewed.text: Continue the same calorie delivery because the initial phosphate was normal
choicesReviewed.review: Normal baseline does not exclude subsequent refeeding physiology.

choicesReviewed.text: Increase calorie delivery to correct the low phosphate without electrolyte treatment
choicesReviewed.review: Increasing calories without electrolyte treatment contradicts response guidance.

choicesReviewed.text: Exclude refeeding because the calories were delivered through a feeding tube
choicesReviewed.review: Tube delivery does not exclude refeeding.

question.question: An adult ICU patient without vasopressor support has a gastric residual of 420 mL, no vomiting, pain, or distention, and stable hemodynamics. The team follows the 2016 SCCM/ASPEN adult ICU guidance. Which interpretation or management plan is most defensible?
choices: Assess the clinical pattern and reinforce aspiration precautions rather than automatically stopping feeding
Treat the value below 500 mL as proof that clinical monitoring can be stopped
Automatically stop feeding until the residual reaches zero despite the stated clinical findings
Use the same rule after new instability or escalating vasopressor needs without reassessment
question.rationale: In this stated setting, the 2016 guideline advises against automatically holding feeding below 500 mL without other intolerance signs. Residuals from 200 to 500 mL still warrant aspiration-risk assessment and preventive measures. Do not interpret a normal examination or this value as a guarantee of safety; reassess if symptoms or hemodynamics change.

choicesReviewed.text: Assess the clinical pattern and reinforce aspiration precautions rather than automatically stopping feeding
choicesReviewed.review: Dated guideline and stable no-vasopressor case support overall clinical assessment/prevention instead of automatic hold.

choicesReviewed.text: Treat the value below 500 mL as proof that clinical monitoring can be stopped
choicesReviewed.review: Below500does not permit stopping clinical monitoring.

choicesReviewed.text: Automatically stop feeding until the residual reaches zero despite the stated clinical findings
choicesReviewed.review: No residual-zero prerequisite in this stated case.

choicesReviewed.text: Use the same rule after new instability or escalating vasopressor needs without reassessment
choicesReviewed.review: New instability/escalating vasopressors changes context and requires reassessment.

teachingReview.heading: Advance according to risk
teachingReview.body: Individualize advancement according to perfusion, gastrointestinal tolerance, access site, nutrition risk, and electrolyte status. A stable patient with an established tube may progress differently from a patient recovering from shock or starting postpyloric feeding. The 2020 ASPEN refeeding consensus recommends checking potassium, magnesium, and phosphate before nutrition begins and delaying initiation or increases in calories when these levels are severely low until corrected. Other low levels in a patient at refeeding risk warrant supplementation and consideration of delaying advancement. Monitor the clinical pattern, glucose, fluid balance, and electrolytes during cautious initiation; a precipitous fall or levels that are difficult to correct require prompt reassessment of energy delivery and electrolyte treatment. Include calories from intravenous dextrose when assessing refeeding exposure rather than advancing by the clock alone.

clauseSource.claim: Severely low baselineK/Mg/phosphate delays calories until corrected; other low levels require correction and considered delay
Count IV dextrose energy; avoid clock-only advancement

teachingReview.heading: Prevent aspiration with a bundle
teachingReview.body: For critically ill adults receiving gastric enteral nutrition, use coordinated aspiration precautions: elevate the head of the bed 30 to 45 degrees when clinically feasible, confirm the intended tube position before use and reassess when migration is suspected, and minimize unnecessary sedation while maintaining appropriate comfort and care. Assess gastric emptying and the patient's ability to protect the airway; consider postpyloric access for high aspiration risk and continuous delivery when gastric boluses are not tolerated. The 2016 SCCM/ASPEN guideline advises against adding blue dye or methylene blue to formula as aspiration markers. A single residual volume does not establish aspiration or normal tolerance. Apply age- and condition-specific positioning guidance rather than transferring this adult ICU bundle to infants.

clauseSource.claim: Confirm intended position before use, suspected-migration reassessment
clauseSource.source: safe2017Q9.2 and previously verified access-safety review

clauseSource.claim: Minimum unnecessary sedation with care; assess airway/emptying
High-risk postpyloric and gastric-bolus-intolerant continuous consideration
Single residual cannot diagnose normal tolerance/aspiration; infant guidance differs

teachingReview.heading: Use gastric residuals selectively
teachingReview.body: The 2016 SCCM/ASPEN adult ICU guideline advises against routine gastric residual volume monitoring and against automatically holding feeding for a residual below 500 mL when other intolerance signs are absent. Values in the 200 to 500 mL range still warrant aspiration-risk assessment and preventive measures. This is not a universal safety cutoff: the 2023 ASPEN practice tool, in its vasopressor-administration guidance, describes a reasonable hold above 300 mL based on limited, low-quality evidence. Follow the applicable clinical setting and institutional protocol rather than combining these thresholds into one rule. Assess residual trends with vomiting, distention, pain, hemodynamics, stool, available imaging, and aspiration risk. Neither a value below 500 mL nor omission of routine residual checks establishes normal tolerance or removes the need for clinical monitoring.

Hold feeding until every residual measurement is zero despite the stable clinical findings

check.rationale: The 2016 adult ICU guideline advises against an automatic hold below 500 mL when other intolerance signs are absent.
